Recommended Hour VMT Distributions To Be Considered for MOVES ............................... 127 xi This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications. 1 Introduction The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) MOtor Vehicle Emission Simulator (MOVES) models mobile sources of air toxics at small and large scales across the Unites States. Vehicle speed distributions based on the type of vehicle, type of road traveled, and hour of the day are inputs into MOVES. In conjunction with vehicle miles traveled (VMT) inputs, they are used to estimate total operation time and select the relevant driving cycles from which running operating modes and emissions are estimated. In an ongoing research effort, the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) partnered with the EPA to provide default average speed data for heavy-duty vehicles based on NLR’s FleetDNA database and the Bourns College of Engineering – Center for Environmental Research and Technology (CE-CERT) data set from the University of California, Riverside. NLR’s FleetDNA is a detailed database of 1-Hz time-series commercial truck and bus data that includes over 2,000 in-use vehicles operating over 12 million miles of driving. FleetDNA data from conventional-fueled vehicles fall into six MOVES source types: combination-unit long-haul trucks, combination-unit short-haul trucks, single-unit short-haul trucks, refuse trucks, transit buses, and school buses. The CE-CERT data were developed for the California Air Resources Board (CARB) in 2017 (Zhang et al. 2021). CE-CERT heavy-duty vehicles fall into five MOVES source types: combination-unit short-haul trucks, single-unit short-haul trucks, refuse trucks, transit buses, and other buses. Excluding the “other bus” source type, which contains airport shuttle buses, the four other source types overlap with observed FleetDNA source types. On a vocational level, CE-CERT contained some line-haul trucks that did not perform multiday trips, and as such were classified as MOVES combination-unit short-haul source rather than long-haul source type (Zhang et al. 2021). Only two vocations overlapped between the two data sets: towing from the single-unit short-haul source type and drayage from the combination-unit short-haul source type. Using these data, we calculated average speeds, the proportion of time spent in different speed ranges, and the proportion of distance spent driving under various MOVES categories. MOVES categories include source type ID (the type of heavy-duty vehicle), road type ID, day ID (weekend – 2 or weekday – 5), and hour ID. EPA uses source types to classify different vehicle categories with similar activity. The heavy-duty vehicle source types are listed in Table 1.
